answer.label: Spoken by
answer.authorDates: b. 1955 · Microsoft co-founder; chief software architect, 2000–2008
answer.sourceLine: Gates said it in a student question-and-answer session during his February 2004 tour of university computer-science departments. The earliest documented printing is Steve Lohr’s report in The New York Times of 1 March 2004 (story starts p. C1; the quotation is on p. C2, col. 6), where it runs “If you invent a breakthrough in artificial intelligence, so machines can learn,” Mr. Gates responded, “that is worth 10 Microsofts” — a citation traced by Quote Investigator, which credits Gates.

source.excerpt: “If you invent a breakthrough in artificial intelligence, so machines can learn,” Mr. Gates responded, “that is worth 10 Microsofts.”
trail: 1 March 2004 — the earliest citation. Quote Investigator gives Steve Lohr’s New York Times piece “Microsoft, Amid Dwindling Interest, Talks Up Computing as a Career” — start page C1, quotation page C2, column 6 — as the first documented printing.

February 2004 — the setting. Gates was midway through a five-campus swing taking in Harvard, MIT, Cornell, Carnegie Mellon and Illinois, according to the Harvard Gazette, arguing that computing was still worth studying after the dot-com crash.
26 April 2004 — the second printing. Investor’s Business Daily ran Patrick Seitz’s report quoting the same answer and placing the exchange at MIT, as reproduced by Quote Investigator.

2009 onward — the drift begins. Quote Investigator logs the remark resurfacing in a Minneapolis paper in January 2009 and, that July, in InformationWeek in the loosened form “a breakthrough in machine learning could be worth 10 Microsofts” — the ancestor of today’s sourceless aggregator version.

source.excerptNote: The question that prompted it, as printed six weeks later by Investor’s Business Daily and quoted by Quote Investigator: at a stop at MIT, a student asked Gates whether another tech company could ever match Microsoft’s success.

author.name: Bill Gates
author.heading: Who said it
author.metaLine: b. 28 October 1955 · Microsoft co-founder; chief software architect, 2000–2008
author.bio: William Henry Gates III co-founded Microsoft and ran it as chief executive until 2000, when he handed the CEO role to Steve Ballmer and became chief software architect, a post he held until 2008. That was his title in February 2004, when he toured a run of American university campuses arguing that computer science was still worth studying after the dot-com crash. The AI line came out of a student Q&A on that tour — an off-the-cuff answer, not a prepared slide, which is part of why it took a researcher with newspaper-database access to pin down where it first appeared in print.

misattribution.heading: Right name, drifting words
misattribution.intro: This is the unusual case on a fact-check site: the famous name actually said it. What has gone wrong is the wording. The version most often pasted online is smoother, shorter and sourceless — and it swaps the term Gates used.

items.who: “A breakthrough in machine learning would be worth ten Microsofts”
items.why: The aggregator form, circulated with no source or date attached. It substitutes “machine learning” for Gates’s “artificial intelligence,” spells out “ten,” and drops the conditional “If you invent…” that made it an answer to a student’s challenge rather than a market forecast.

items.who: “a breakthrough in machine learning could be worth 10 Microsofts”
items.why: How the line already appeared in InformationWeek in July 2009, per the citation list assembled by Quote Investigator. The “machine learning” substitution is old, and it is where the modern aggregator wording most likely comes from.

The commonly circulated form runs the clause together. The New York Times text has a comma — “artificial intelligence, so machines can learn” — while the unpunctuated version matches what Investor’s Business Daily printed in April 2004, both reproduced by Quote Investigator.

misattribution.truthLine: The attribution is sound. Quote Investigator concludes that Bill Gates should be credited with the quotation as given in the 1 March 2004 New York Times article — if you want the exact words, use that version, with its comma.

context.heading: Why he was on a campus stage at all
lead: The dot-com crash had done something Microsoft found genuinely alarming: it scared students off. As Quote Investigator sets the scene, wary undergraduates watched internet stock prices collapse and the number of computer science majors fell, so in 2004 Gates went on the road to tell them the opportunities were still there. The Harvard Gazette counted five campuses on the swing: Harvard, MIT, Cornell, Carnegie Mellon and Illinois.

The “10 Microsofts” line was not the speech. It was the answer to a heckle-adjacent student question — could any company ever match what Microsoft had done? — and Gates chose to answer it by naming the prize rather than defending the record. Machines that learn, he said, would be worth an order of magnitude more than the company he built.
context.detailsSummary: What Gates was saying on the rest of the tour
detailsBody: Artificial intelligence was a running theme, not a one-off. At Carnegie Mellon he lectured on “Software Breakthroughs: Solving the Toughest Problems in Computer Science” on 25 February and praised the university’s work in artificial intelligence and speech recognition. At Cornell he named developing AI as, in the Cornell Chronicle’s account, the ultimate in computer science achievement.

The line has had a long second life. Quote Investigator records it resurfacing in a Minneapolis newspaper in January 2009 and in InformationWeek that July, and it has been recycled steadily since by investment writers whenever machine learning is back in the headlines — usually with the 2004 setting stripped off.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator gives the earliest documented citation as The New York Times, 1 March 2004, "Microsoft, Amid Dwindling Interest, Talks Up Computing as a Career" by Steve Lohr, start page C1, quote page C2, column 6, and concludes Bill Gates should be credited with the quotation.
Quote Investigator reproduces the New York Times wording as: "If you invent a breakthrough in artificial intelligence, so machines can learn," Mr. Gates responded, "that is worth 10 Microsofts."

Quote Investigator's block quotation from Investor's Business Daily (26 April 2004, Patrick Seitz, page A01) includes the sentence "In a stop at MIT, a student asked Gates if another tech company could ever match Microsoft's success."

Quote Investigator lists later citations in the Minneapolis Examiner (27 January 2009) and InformationWeek (6 July 2009), the latter in the paraphrased form "a breakthrough in machine learning could be worth 10 Microsofts".

Quote Investigator's narrative states that after the dot-com crash the number of computer science majors declined and that in 2004 Bill Gates visited a series of universities to encourage students to pursue a career in computing.

The Harvard Gazette (published March 2004) reports Gates speaking at Harvard as part of a five-campus tour that also included MIT, Cornell, Carnegie Mellon and the University of Illinois, and notes his remark that fewer people were working in artificial intelligence than twenty years earlier.

Carnegie Mellon's news page records Gates's first campus visit on Feb. 25 with the lecture "Software Breakthroughs: Solving the Toughest Problems in Computer Science" and his praise for the university's work in artificial intelligence and speech recognition; it does not contain the phrase "10 Microsofts".
The Cornell Chronicle's 2004 report on Gates's visit describes developing AI as the ultimate in computer science achievement, and does not contain "10 Microsofts".
An MIT World mailing-list announcement states that Bill Gates came to MIT in February to talk about the next generation of software and the challenges facing the software industry.
AZQuotes hosts the wording "A breakthrough in machine learning would be worth ten Microsofts." credited to Bill Gates with no source, publication or date given.
Wikipedia gives Bill Gates's birth date as 28 October 1955 and states that after Steve Ballmer succeeded him as CEO in 2000 he became chief software architect, a position he held until 2008.
Wikiquote's Bill Gates page does not contain the "10 Microsofts" quotation in any section.

The Motley Fool (24 August 2019) quotes Gates as saying "If you invent a breakthrough in artificial intelligence, so machines can learn, that is worth 10 Microsofts," attributing it to a 2004 remark to college students reported by The New York Times.
